steps.body: In a word problem, identify the quantities and operation before calculating. The addition model renames unlike fractions and then combines equal-sized pieces.
steps.narration: In a word problem, identify the quantities and operation before calculating. The addition model renames unlike fractions and then combines equal-sized pieces.

widget.prompt: A jug holds 5/12 litre and 4/12 more is poured in. Build the total.
widget.successFeedback: 9/12 litre — five twelfths and four more, counted together.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 9/12 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 9/12 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: Sixths are the wrong piece size here; pouring twelfths in leaves the total in twelfths.
1/12 is the difference between the two amounts, not their total.

predict.prompt: 'Poured in' means the total will be…
predict.reveal: Adding liquid raises the total above each amount that went into it.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u story.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u story a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Once renamed, a jug holds 3/6 litre and then 2/6 litre more. Express the total as ?/6. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 names the piece size; once the pieces match, only the COUNT of them changes.
That count of pieces does not follow once both fractions wear the same denominator.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.

steps.body: The operation comes from the story: amounts poured in add, while amounts poured out subtract. The subtraction model crosses out the removed pieces.
steps.narration: The operation comes from the story: amounts poured in add, while amounts poured out subtract. The subtraction model crosses out the removed pieces.

widget.prompt: Once renamed, 5/6 litre were available and 2/6 litre was poured out. Express what is left as ?/6. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: That joined the two amounts; pouring out removes pieces rather than adding them.
6 names the piece size, which never changes — only how many are left.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.

widget.prompt: A jug gains one sixth and then three sixths. How many sixth-size parts are there altogether?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 names the piece size; once the pieces match, only the COUNT of them changes.
Multiplying the counts is not joining them — 1 piece and 3 more make 4.

concept.body: The mathematics is unchanged. Only the job of spotting which fractions are being combined, and in which direction, is new.
concept.narration: The mathematics is unchanged. Only the job of spotting which fractions are being combined, and in which direction, is new.

commonErrors.feedback: That joined the two amounts; pouring out removes pieces rather than adding them.
12 names the piece size, which never changes — only how many are left.
